summary:
Vela is a map-first web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge category Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. Designed for satellite land and wildfire analysis, Vela enables users to draw or search for a plot of land anywhere worldwide, select a date, and inspect satellite heat observations, weather outlooks, weekly activity trends, and research methodology scoped to their exact land boundary in a single panel without leaving the map.

Vela addresses the challenge by explicitly keeping active satellite heat detections (from Aqua MODIS, Suomi-NPP VIIRS, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21), fire-danger weather ratings (GWIS/ECMWF), weekly activity trends, and official reports as separate, transparent data streams. Rather than collapsing sensor data into misleading black-box risk scores, Vela integrates a leakage-free machine learning framework—featuring split-before-clean preprocessing, standardized continuous features, multi-model evaluation (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, SVM, Decision Trees, XGBoost) using F1-score/ROC-AUC metrics, and continuous probability heatmaps (0.0 to 1.0). When high wildfire risk is predicted, Vela automatically dispatches SMTP email alerts to local emergency responders.

By presenting raw observations alongside honest limitations and resilient ML engineering, Vela delivers dependable, scientifically grounded insights that build public and technical trust in Earth observation data.
details:
A. What does it do or how does it work?

  • Map Interaction & Polygon Clipping: Users draw custom land boundaries or search for locations worldwide (via OpenStreetMap Nominatim), select an observation date, and click "Check my land". NASA FIRMS active fire detections are clipped precisely to the drawn boundary. Switching panel tabs preserves the polygon boundary, zoom level, selected 5 km square, observation date, satellite filters, and trend year.
    1. Where is this?: Groups detections into 5 km grid squares, visually encoding satellite agreement (circle = 1 satellite, square = 2+ satellites). Clicking a square reveals local/UTC observation times, satellite names, and raw detections.
    2. Weather outlook: Displays point weather forecasts near the land center, including air temperature (°C), relative humidity (%), wind speed/gusts/direction, rainfall accumulation (mm), and numerical Fire Weather Index (FWI) ratings from GWIS ECMWF.
    3. Weekly trends: Provides plain-language annual findings and a compact calendar showing how frequently 5 km grid squares showed burning activity during a selected year.
    4. Research: Explains technical methodology, satellite coverage rules, FWI calculation sources, validation rules, and offers a step-by-step grid square walkthrough.
  • Machine Learning Pipeline & Continuous Heatmap: Preprocesses environmental data using strict split-before-clean protocol and feature standardization. Trains a lineup of models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, SVM, Decision Trees, XGBoost) and selects top performers based on F1-score/ROC-AUC and train/CV/test parity to eliminate overfitting. Predicts continuous probability values (0.0 to 1.0) rendered as a shaded map heatmap to prevent Simpson's Paradox.
  • Automated Responder Alerts: Integrates an automated backend notification module that dispatches email alerts via SMTP directly to local emergency responders when predicted wildfire probability exceeds risk thresholds.
  • Architecture: A Leaflet single-page map frontend communicates with a Python FastAPI backend (/api/check-land, /api/preparedness, /api/calendar, /api/place, /api/trace), backed by modular Python packages for spatial grid pairing, land checks, metrics serving, and notification dispatch.

B. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero Map Context Loss: Users seamlessly switch between active satellite observations, weather forecasts, multi-year activity trends, and scientific documentation without losing their map position or drawn polygon.
  • Scientific Transparency: Keeps satellite heat, weather ratings, weekly trends, and official reports strictly separate rather than producing arbitrary black-box risk scores.
  • Leakage-Free Predictive Analytics: Prevents data leakage by performing dataset splitting prior to cleaning and using training-set medians for test-set imputation.
  • Continuous Risk Visualization: Uses continuous gradient heatmaps (0.0 to 1.0) rather than crude binary high/low flags, avoiding Simpson's Paradox and preserving micro-level spatial risk patterns.
  • Automated Emergency Dispatch: Closes the operational loop by automatically alerting local responders via SMTP when high risk is detected.
  • Honest Error & Gap Handling: Clearly distinguishes empty satellite returns from confirmed clear days, explicitly labels missing weather metrics, and tags uncalibrated satellite readings (e.g., NOAA-20/21 calibration pending status) while isolating API faults so weather service drops never erase heat markers.
  • Localized Context: Supports localized place naming (e.g., barangay → city/municipality → province for Philippine selections) and aligns forecast dates with local timezones (e.g., Asia/Manila).

C. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Empowering Local Land Check & Responder Action: Gives landowners, community managers, emergency teams, and researchers actionable spatial insights clipped directly to their land boundaries, paired with automated emergency responder notifications.
  • Demystifying Remote Sensing & ML: Educates users on satellite sensor resolution differences, satellite pass timing, fire weather indices, and transparent machine learning practices to foster greater public trust and scientific understanding of satellite data harmonization.

D. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages & Core Frameworks: Python 3 (FastAPI server, Uvicorn, custom vela package), JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3.
    • NASA FIRMS API (Active fire/hotspot detections from Aqua MODIS, Suomi-NPP VIIRS, NOAA-20 VIIRS, NOAA-21 VIIRS).
    • NASA Earthdata (earthaccess library for downloading raw HDF/NetCDF swath granules).
    • Open-Meteo API (Live point weather forecasts).
    • GWIS / Copernicus EMS ECMWF (Numerical Fire Weather Index ratings).
    • ASMC / Malaysian Meteorological Department (FDRS maps for regional reference).
    • SMTP Notification Module (Automated responder email alerts).

E. How is your project creative?

  • Four-Question Framework: Replaces dense GIS layer lists with four intuitive, human-centered questions (Where is this?, Weather outlook, Weekly trends, Research) embedded directly into the map interface.
  • Geometric Ember Visual Encoding: Uses distinct marker geometry (circles vs. squares) to immediately indicate single vs. multi-satellite agreement across 5 km grid cells.
  • Continuous Probability Heatmap Layer: Renders continuous machine learning risk outputs as smooth, shaded heatmaps rather than binary flags, giving visual clarity without masking localized risk nuances.
  • Automated Emergency Dispatch Loop: Connects real-time satellite data harmonization and machine learning risk predictions directly to automated SMTP responder alerts.

F. What factors did your team consider?

  • Data Leakage Prevention: Strictly enforced dataset splitting before data cleaning or imputation, using training-set parameters (e.g., medians) to process test data.
  • Continuous Variable Standardization: Scaled continuous environmental features (temperature, wind speed, humidity, heat index) onto identical scales so linear models treat all inputs equally.
  • Imbalanced Dataset Evaluation: Evaluated model performance using F1-score and ROC-AUC rather than misleading raw accuracy, given that wildfire hotspots are rare events.
  • Overfitting Elimination & Model Selection: Evaluated a full model lineup (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, SVM, Decision Trees, XGBoost) and selected top performers by verifying performance parity across training, cross-validation (CV), and test sets.
  • Avoiding Simpson's Paradox: Used continuous probability heatmaps (0.0 to 1.0) instead of aggregate binary risk tags to preserve localized spatial risk patterns.
  • Fault Isolation & Localization: Engineered backend services so that weather API timeouts never hide active satellite heat markers, while tailoring place hierarchies and timezones for regional relevance.
